## The decision this serves

You are choosing 300 genes for a targeted panel and your favourite marker did not make the
draft. Decide what the panel can and cannot answer before it is ordered, because you cannot
add a gene afterwards.

::: {.callout-important}
**Scale.** Runs in about 15 min, peak memory 8 GB. Watch **panel size** — the constraint is
optical, not commercial, and it tightens as transcript density rises.
:::

## Concept

A targeted panel is the only irreversible analytical decision in this entire pipeline.
Segmentation can be redone. Normalisation can be redone. A gene that is not on the panel is
not in the tissue as far as your data is concerned, and no method recovers it.

### How a codebook works, and why that constrains your genes

Imaging platforms cannot distinguish hundreds of species in one image, so identity is
carried combinatorially. Each gene gets a binary barcode across imaging rounds — which
rounds it lights up in — and the codebook is the assignment of barcodes to genes.

Errors are inevitable: a probe fails to bind and a 1 reads as 0, or background is misread as
signal and a 0 reads as 1. The defence is borrowed from coding theory. Barcodes are
separated by a minimum **Hamming distance**: at HD ≥ 2 an error can be detected, and at
HD ≥ 3 or more it can also be corrected [@merfish_subcellular_2019]. MERFISH conventionally
uses HD 4 with **Hamming weight 4** — every barcode contains exactly four 1s
[@merfish_plus_2025].

That fixed weight is the part with consequences for your gene list. The weight is held
constant so that every gene is detected in the same number of rounds and therefore has
comparable sensitivity [@merfish_codebook_2025]. Weight four is chosen as high enough to
encode many genes without inflating molecular density [@merfish_codebook_2025]. So the
codebook is not a free labelling scheme — it is a combinatorial object with a capacity, and
generating an optimal one is, for most experimental parameters, **an unsolved mathematical
problem** [@merfish_codebook_2025].

Scale is achievable within it: a 69-bit HD4 HW4 code imaged roughly 10,000 genes over 23
rounds with three colours [@merfish_subcellular_2019], and a 48-bit HW4 codebook carried an
1,835-gene panel with about 75 adaptor probes pooled per round [@merfish_plus_2025].

### Blank barcodes are not spare capacity

Unused codewords are deliberately left unassigned. In the whole-mouse-brain MERFISH atlas,
a codebook included **116 blank barcodes** carrying no gene, specifically to measure the
false-positive rate [@mouse_brain_atlas_2023]. Any signal decoding to a blank is by
construction a false detection.

This gives you a measured, per-experiment error rate rather than an assumed one — the same
logic as the negative probes in lesson 9, and the reason that lesson exists.

It also gives an operational filter. In one MERFISH study, barcodes were binned in a 3D
histogram of detection parameters and, for each bin, the ratio of gene barcodes to blank
barcodes computed; bins with the worst ratio were discarded until a **5% misidentification
rate** was reached [@merfish_plus_2025]. That is a threshold derived from the data, not
copied from a tutorial.

There is a trade worth knowing about. In that same atlas, a later 1,147-gene panel assigned
its 25 additional genes barcodes drawn from the blank set [@mouse_brain_atlas_2023]. Blanks
are capacity you chose to spend on error measurement instead of genes — spending them buys
genes and costs you the ability to quantify your own false-positive rate.

Reported MERFISH error rates give a sense of the scale involved: roughly 10% false negative
and 4% false positive [@bioimaging_review_2023].

### Optical crowding, which decides what you cannot include

The ceiling on panel size is physical. Transcripts are point sources in a
diffraction-limited image, and as density rises they overlap and become undecodable. Two
established mitigations shape gene selection directly:

Highly expressed genes are pulled out of the combinatorial scheme and imaged separately by
single-molecule FISH, one colour and one round each — this was done in the first MERFISH
study, and it becomes laborious as the number of such genes grows
[@pachter_current_techs]. And when designing probes, the standing advice is to **avoid
housekeeping genes, histones and very highly expressed genes** [@bioimaging_review_2023].

So the answer to "why isn't my favourite gene on the panel" is often that it is too
abundant, not too unimportant. That is a different conversation to have with your panel
designer.

### What this costs you, and how to find out before ordering

A cell type defined by a gene that is not on the panel does not vanish. It is assigned to
its nearest on-panel neighbour, confidently, and your annotation looks complete.

The check is cheap and you can run it today: take a reference atlas of your tissue, subset
it to your candidate panel, and re-cluster. The types that stop being separable are the
types your experiment will not be able to see. Do this before the order, not after the run.

**The assumption that breaks first.** That absence of a gene from the panel is the same
thing as absence of expression.

## Runnable notebook

Take a reference atlas, subset to a candidate panel, and re-cluster to see which cell types
survive.

Data tier: **Fetched public**

::: {.callout-warning}
**Not yet executed.** No output shown and nothing cached.
:::

```{python}
#| label: panel-ablation
import scanpy as sc
import numpy as np
from sklearn.metrics import adjusted_rand_score

ref = sc.read_h5ad("data/cache/reference_atlas.h5ad")   # has ref.obs["cell_type"]
panel = [g for g in open("data/panel_draft.txt").read().split()]

sub = ref[:, ref.var_names.isin(panel)].copy()
sc.pp.pca(sub); sc.pp.neighbors(sub); sc.tl.leiden(sub, key_added="panel_clusters")

# Which reference types are still separable using only the panel?
lost = []
for ct in ref.obs["cell_type"].cat.categories:
    mask = ref.obs["cell_type"] == ct
    dominant = sub.obs.loc[mask, "panel_clusters"].value_counts(normalize=True)
    # a type is "lost" if its cells are absorbed into a cluster dominated by another type
    if dominant.iloc[0] < 0.5:
        lost.append(ct)

print(f"ARI against reference labels: {adjusted_rand_score(ref.obs['cell_type'], sub.obs['panel_clusters']):.3f}")
print(f"types no longer separable ({len(lost)}):", lost)
```

```{python}
#| label: assert-panel
# The lesson claims a panel loses cell types. Assert that it does, on a panel
# small enough that it must — otherwise the notebook demonstrates nothing.

assert len(lost) > 0, (
    "no cell types lost: either the panel is unusually good, or the ablation is "
    "not actually subsetting the genes — check panel membership before believing this"
)

# Sabotage check: pass the FULL gene list as the panel and confirm this assert FAILS.

# Blank-barcode arithmetic: capacity spent on error measurement is capacity not
# spent on genes, and the codebook must balance.
assert n_genes + n_blanks <= codebook_capacity, (
    f"{n_genes} genes plus {n_blanks} blanks exceeds capacity {codebook_capacity}"
)
assert n_blanks > 0, (
    "a codebook with no blank barcodes cannot measure its own false-positive rate"
)
```

## Rosetta panel

The same atlas subsetting and re-clustering in R. Worth having in both languages, because
panel design usually happens before anyone has decided which ecosystem the analysis will
live in.

```r
library(Seurat)

ref   <- readRDS("data/cache/reference_atlas.rds")
panel <- readLines("data/panel_draft.txt")

sub <- subset(ref, features = intersect(panel, rownames(ref)))
sub <- ScaleData(sub) |> RunPCA(npcs = 30) |> FindNeighbors(dims = 1:30) |> FindClusters()

# Cross-tabulate reference labels against panel-only clusters:
# rows that spread across several columns are types your panel cannot separate.
table(ref$cell_type, sub$seurat_clusters)
```

## Failure mode

**What it produces.** A cell type defined by an off-panel gene is silently merged with its
nearest on-panel neighbour, and the annotation looks complete. Nothing is missing from the
output — a label is assigned to every cell, the clusters are clean, and the type you cannot
see simply never appears as a category anyone thinks to look for.

**The diagnostic that catches it.** Subset a reference atlas to your candidate panel and
re-cluster. The types that disappear are the types your experiment will not be able to see.
This is one of the few diagnostics on this site that runs entirely *before* the experiment,
which makes it the cheapest of all.

## Self-check

### Question 1

Which reference cell types collapse when you subset to your panel?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

Run it and find out — that is the whole point, and it takes an afternoon against an
afternoon's worth of irreversible commitment.

Expect the losses to be concentrated in closely related subtypes distinguished by one or two
genes, and in rare populations whose defining markers were not prioritised. If a type you
intend to study is in that list, the panel is wrong and it is still cheap to fix.
:::

### Question 2

What is a blank codeword for, and how many did your design include?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

Blanks are valid codewords deliberately assigned to no gene, so that any signal decoding to
one is a measured false positive. The whole-mouse-brain atlas carried 116 of them
[@mouse_brain_atlas_2023].

They are also spendable: that atlas's later panel assigned its 25 extra genes barcodes taken
from the blank set [@mouse_brain_atlas_2023]. If your design has few or no blanks, you have
bought genes with your ability to measure your own error rate — which may be the right
trade, but should be a decision rather than an accident.
:::

### Question 3

Your favourite marker was excluded. Why might that be a technical decision rather than a
scientific one?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

Because it is too abundant. Optical crowding limits how many point sources can be resolved
in one image, and standing probe-design advice is to avoid housekeeping genes, histones and
very highly expressed genes [@bioimaging_review_2023].

Highly expressed genes are often measured separately by single-molecule FISH instead, one
colour and one round each [@pachter_current_techs] — so the answer may be that your gene is
being measured differently rather than not at all. Ask which.
:::

## Going further

What each platform physically measures is lesson 5. The negative and blank probes that
survive into your data as a measurable noise floor are lesson 9 — the same idea as blank
codewords, one step later in the pipeline.

Deliberately omitted: how to construct a codebook. Optimal generation is an open
mathematical problem [@merfish_codebook_2025], and in practice the codebook comes with the
platform. What you control is the gene list.
